Week twelve, Tuesday: Usha, a bank analyst, finished the day's work at nine, then spent until one in the morning on the literacy project's spreadsheets. Her eyes stung and her hands shook from too much tea. Next morning she missed a step at her desk, and that evening Ayesha, a volunteer, found her asleep at the project table.

Saturday: Usha sat with Ayesha and said, 'If I burn out, the project stops. It's only worth doing if I'm still here in two years.' She wrote a limit: Tuesday and Saturday, three hours each, and one week off every month.

Two weeks later: Usha put out a call on the neighbourhood group and six new people came. She left at eight on Tuesday, tired in a normal way, and for the first time did not check her phone.

qa.q: How many hours did Usha set for each of Tuesday and Saturday?
qa.a: Usha set three hours for each.

qa.q: What is Usha afraid of when saying 'If I burn out, the project stops'?
qa.a: Usha is afraid the project would collapse if she wore herself out, and she wants it to last longer than her energy.

qa.q: What other step could Usha take besides limiting her hours?
qa.a: Usha could hand the spreadsheets to one of the new volunteers, since sharing the late-night tasks protects both her health and the project.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have felt on finding Usha asleep at the table?
qa.a: Ayesha was probably worried and concerned, seeing how tired Usha had become.

grounding: Shows a person noticing burnout after months of late nights, limiting the project to fixed weekly hours and inviting more volunteers.

Vidya, sit, let me tell you about your Nilesh Chacha at twenty-five. I worked at the bank all day and ran a night school for mill workers' children from seven to ten. Three months of that. I ate dinner at midnight, and I was so proud of myself.
Then one afternoon I fell asleep at my counter while a customer was counting notes. My manager woke me, not angrily, just worried. That shook me more than a scolding would have.
That night I sat with a notebook and asked myself a plain question. If I break, who teaches those children? Nobody. So I cut the school to Tuesday and Saturday, two hours each, and I asked two college boys from our street to take the other days.
The school ran eleven more years, beti. It would not have lasted one more winter with me running it alone.

qa.q: How long did Nilesh run the night school every evening before things changed?
qa.a: For three months Nilesh ran it from seven to ten, eating dinner at midnight.

qa.q: What did Nilesh feel after the manager woke him at the counter?
qa.a: Nilesh felt shaken, because the manager's worry, more than any scolding, showed how worn out the long nights had made him.

qa.q: At the moment he sat with the notebook, what other choice could Nilesh have made, and how might it have gone?
qa.a: Nilesh could have pushed on alone out of pride, but would likely have broken down within the winter and the school would have closed.

qa.q: How might the two college boys from the street have seen the invitation to teach?
qa.a: They may have felt trusted and proud to be asked, and their joining is what let the school keep going for eleven more years.

grounding: It shows a young man noticing burnout after months of late nights, fixing limited weekly hours and inviting more volunteers so the project can last.

The rain had turned the municipal ground to mud again, and Wasim stood under the tin shed with twenty boys and girls waiting for football practice. It was the third wet Saturday in a row. He had a fever and a report due for his office on Monday.
For three months he had worked till eight, planned drills till one in the morning, and coached every weekend. He was always tired now, snapping at kids for small mistakes.
He looked at the muddy ground and thought it through. If I keep this up, I'll quit by December, and then they have nobody.
That evening he called Ira, a former college goalkeeper who had once offered to help. "Saturdays are mine, eight to ten. Could you take Sundays?"
Ira laughed. "I thought you'd never ask."
Wasim wrote the hours on the shed wall in chalk and went home to sleep.

qa.q: What did Wasim write on the shed wall?
qa.a: He wrote the hours on the shed wall in chalk.

qa.q: What was Wasim feeling as he looked at the muddy ground?
qa.a: He felt exhausted and worried, since he had been snapping at the children and feared he would quit by December.

qa.q: Which approach could also have helped Wasim, and why?
qa.a: He could ask a parent to handle scheduling and messages, since planning drills late at night was draining him as much as the coaching.

qa.q: How might the children at practice be affected by Wasim's new plan?
qa.a: They get a calmer coach and a second coach on Sundays, so practice is less likely to stop suddenly when he is tired or ill.

grounding: It shows a young man with a job noticing burnout after three months of late nights, limiting his coaching hours and bringing in another volunteer.
